claims.text: Atomic-scale interactions and grain-boundary effects govern the premelting and melting behavior of high-entropy-alloy nanoparticles.
Atomic-scale interactions and grain-boundary effects influence nanoparticle surface energy.
Nanoparticle surface energy governs thermal stability.
Bond breaking and formation, diffusion, and defect migration are relevant atomic-scale mediators of premelting and melting.
Changes in surface energy caused by atomic interactions and grain-boundary effects change premelting onset temperature.
Changes in surface energy caused by atomic interactions and grain-boundary effects change the melting point.
Decreasing nanoparticle size relative to a 20 nm baseline will lower the melting point by 100-200 K.
Increasing surface modification relative to an unmodified baseline will lower the melting point by 100-200 K.
Decreasing nanoparticle size will increase premelting behavior by 10-20% relative to the baseline.
Increasing surface modification will increase premelting behavior by 10-20% relative to the baseline.
The comparison baseline is an unmodified, 20 nm, equimolar CoCrFeMnNi nanoparticle.
The proposed simulation uses temperatures of 300-1500 K, a pressure of 1 atm, and a simulation duration of 100 ns.
The hypothesized behavior is expected to hold for particle sizes from 5 to 50 nm.
The hypothesized behavior is expected to hold from 300 to 2000 K.
The hypothesized behavior is expected to hold for high-entropy alloys containing 5-15 elements.
Particle shape, defects, and impurities may influence the roles of surface energy, grain boundaries, and atomic-scale interactions.
Changes smaller than 50 K in melting point and 5% in premelting behavior would falsify the hypothesis.
Failure of size, composition, or surface modification to significantly affect surface energy would falsify the hypothesis.
